implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: force the compiler to collapse a call into its call site. Three variants, in increasing force: (1) a priority hint that raises the function's inlining score so it beats the cost budget; (2) a mandatory form (C++ __attribute__((always_inline)), Rust #[inline(always)], Kotlin @_alwaysInline) that overrides the budget entirely - use only where the profile says the call dominates; (3) manual inlining, copying the body at the call site, which is almost always wrong because it duplicates the logic. The discipline: measure first, confirm the cost is call overhead rather than memory or I/O, and re-check the instruction-cache footprint afterwards because a body that no longer fits makes the loop slower. Prefer the compile-time variants over manual inlining so the abstraction survives.
idiom_name: inline hint (priority) / always_inline (mandatory) / manual body copy (last resort)
code_sketch:
# The three variants, and what each is for.

# 1. PRIORITY HINT: raises the score so a small hot function beats the budget.
#    This is the default tool, and the one that is safe to apply broadly to
#    small cross-boundary helpers (getters, comparisons, generic instantiations).
inline_fn: pass the hint

# 2. MANDATORY: overrides the budget. Use only where the profile shows the call
#    dominating, and RE-MEASURE the instruction footprint afterwards: a body that
#    exceeds the i-cache makes the loop slower than the call it replaced.
always_inline_fn: the one measured hot path

# 3. MANUAL: copy the body at the call site. Almost always wrong - it duplicates
#    the logic so every future fix must be applied at every copy.
{ /* pasted body */ sum += a[i].value; if (a[i].w > 0) sum += a[i].w; }  # don't
pitfalls: A declined inline is usually the compiler's cost model being right - forcing it overrides a better-informed decision.
The instruction cache is the limit: a hot loop that no longer fits fetches instructions from memory, and every arithmetic optimisation inside it is wasted.
Taking the function's address anywhere prevents inlining - the body is still emitted, so the hint buys nothing and the code is duplicated anyway.
Manual inlining duplicates the logic and makes every change cross-cutting; prefer the compile-time hint so the abstraction survives.
